justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I'll assume was a baseline near 395–397 at the time of forecasting. For the 1-day horizon, the estimate of 397 essentially anchors on near-term price continuity, assuming no major catalysts and typical overnight/session drift patterns. The 1-week estimate of 400 builds in a slight positive bias, consistent with a general tendency for equity indices to drift upward over short horizons in the absence of clear negative signals. The 1-month estimate of 410 extends that logic further, reflecting a rough annualized return assumption in the mid-single digits applied over roughly four weeks, while acknowledging that medium-term mean reversion and macro conditions were relatively neutral at the time.

The confidence interval widths expand as they should across horizons, but the specific calibration reflects the typical realized volatility of whatever underlying instrument this tracks — likely an ETF or index near the 400 level such as SPY. Daily moves of roughly plus or minus 1% imply a roughly 4-point range at one standard deviation for a single day, so the 90% interval of 378–416 captures roughly two to two-and-a-half standard deviations of daily movement. At one week, volatility scales by the square root of time, widening the interval to 365–435, and at one month further still to 340–480, reflecting the compounding uncertainty of roughly 21 trading days.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside those stated intervals include a sudden shift in Federal Reserve policy signaling — either an unexpected rate hike or a pivot — which historically produces outsized single-day moves in equity markets. Geopolitical shocks, a surprise in inflation or employment data, or a credit event in a systemically important institution could all generate tail moves beyond what historical volatility alone would suggest. Liquidity conditions also matter: in thin markets, gap moves can exceed what a normal distribution predicts.

It is also worth acknowledging model limitations. My intervals assume something close to log-normal price dynamics with relatively stable volatility, but realized volatility is itself uncertain and can spike sharply. If implied volatility were elevated at the time of the forecast — as it is during earnings seasons or macro event clusters — the true uncertainty would be wider than my stated intervals, meaning I may have been underconfident at the tails while being reasonably calibrated near the center.
